title: To be understood
hookLine: the first truth's task is to be understood, not fixed or blamed (SN 56.11)

cards: When something hurts, two buttons are within easy reach. The first says fix it: take something, buy something, change the plan, make it stop. The second says blame it: whose fault is this, mine or theirs?
Both buttons are fast. Both feel like doing something. In the first sermon, the Buddha gives the first truth a job, and it isn't either button.
He says this truth is to be understood.

teach.b: In the first sermon, each truth comes with a task; over the coming week, the other three.

teach.h: PARIÑÑEYYA: KNOWN ALL THE WAY AROUND.
teach.b: The first truth's task, in Pali, is pariññeyya: to be fully understood, known all the way around. Pali dictionaries read pari as around or fully, joined to the verb to know.
Picture a boulder fallen across your path, and walking all the way around it, looking from every side, before you try to move it. Notice what the Buddha doesn't say.

He doesn't say dukkha is to be fixed; the sermon gives the job of letting go to the second truth, the cause, not to the pain itself. He doesn't say it's to be blamed, on you or anyone. He doesn't say ignore it, either.
He says understand it. That changes how a bad moment feels from the inside. A pain you're fighting has two parts: the pain, and the fight.
A pain you're studying, gently, with curiosity, has a little room around it.
Now the week, from the top. It opened with the elephant's footprint, Sariputta's picture of the four truths holding every good teaching. Then a physician's pattern: illness, cause, cure, treatment.
Then the first truth in full: birth, aging, sickness, death, not getting what you want. Then three kinds of dukkha: pain, change, and the unease of made things. And today, what to do with all of it.

how: In meditation, many Buddhists are taught to turn toward discomfort and investigate it, noting where it is and how it changes, rather than reacting to it at once.

o: to be fixed and cleared away as fast as you can
to be endured quietly, as something deserved
to be fully understood, known from every side

games.q: match each day of this week to what it gave.
p: the four truths hold every teaching

s: in the first sermon, the first truth's task is to be ended
its task is to be understood; letting go is the task of the second truth, the cause.
each of the four truths is given its own task
the first sermon gives each truth a job; this week we met the first.
understanding a pain means agreeing that you deserve it
the task isn't blame of anyone; it's knowing the pain fully, from every side.

games.q: a pain shows up: a hard phone call. you can fix it fast, find someone to blame, or do the first truth's task. which is the first truth's task?
games.why: the first sermon says the truth of dukkha is to be fully understood: known all the way around before anything else.

practice: Choose one small pain, in the body or the heart, and instead of pushing it away or asking whose fault it is, walk around it: where exactly is it, is it sharp or dull, heavy or hot, does it shift from breath to breath?
Look at it the way you'd study a stone in your hand. If it gets too much, come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Pariññeyya. To be fully understood, known all the way around: the task the first sermon gives to dukkha, not fixed in a hurry, not blamed.

orig.note: Pali pariññeyya: to be fully understood, the task the first sermon gives the first truth.

carryVoice: Your line: understand it. Before the fix and before the blame, there's room to look. One week of year two, done.

sources.ref: SN 56.11 (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta), the tasks of the four truths
